name: Leukocyte-poor PRP

card.summary: A platelet-rich plasma preparation spun to contain few white blood cells, used in aesthetic and hair-restoration clinics on the idea that growth factors from platelets support tissue renewal.
card.note: Preparation methods vary widely between kits and clinics; FDA regulates the devices rather than PRP itself.

quick.overview:
Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is made from a person's own blood, spun to concentrate platelets. Leukocyte-poor PRP is a version in which white blood cells are largely removed, a distinction researchers use to classify preparations [1].

The appearance payoff is that clinics use PRP for scalp hair thinning and skin rejuvenation, on the idea that platelet growth factors encourage healing and growth. The best-studied use is joint injection, where a 2024 randomized trial reported that leukocytes did not change safety or efficacy in knee osteoarthritis [3].
quick.how: In a clinic, blood is drawn, processed in a centrifuge or kit, and the resulting plasma is injected or applied, sometimes with microneedling. The number of sessions and kit type depend on the clinic.
quick.risks: Side effects are generally limited to injection-site pain and swelling, with infection risk when equipment is not sterile. The FDA does not regulate PRP itself, though preparation devices are cleared.

lead: Leukocyte-poor PRP, also called leukocyte-reduced or pure PRP, is a platelet concentrate prepared from a person's own blood in which white blood cells are removed or minimized. A 2009 classification paper sorted platelet concentrates by leukocyte and fibrin content, listing pure PRP as a separate category from leukocyte-rich PRP and fibrin products [2].

People encounter PRP in aesthetic and hair-restoration clinics, where platelets' growth factors are used for scalp thinning and skin rejuvenation [4]. Platelet growth factors are reported to support healing [1].
Research on leukocyte content comes mainly from orthopedics. A 2024 randomized trial concluded leukocytes did not influence safety or efficacy of PRP for knee osteoarthritis [3].

chain: Own blood is spun to concentrate platelets
Growth factors delivered to scalp or skin
Supports follicle and tissue renewal (as claimed)
angle.text: Clinics apply PRP to the scalp or face hoping to thicken hair or refresh skin. The leukocyte-poor variant is chosen by providers who prefer a purer platelet product.

infobox: Devices cleared; PRP itself not regulated

paras: PRP preparation kits differ in platelet concentration and leukocyte content, and a review found no consensus on optimal concentrations and no validated classification [1]. Leukocyte-poor products are one category in published classification systems [2].

PRP is discussed in hair-loss and facial-rejuvenation settings as a clinic-based option, often with microneedling. Within these discussions, the leukocyte-poor preparation is one of several kit types.
Trials in joints report mainly injection-site discomfort [3]. A 2024 case in which unlicensed equipment reuse was linked to infections shows sterile technique matters [4].

Most randomized trials of leukocyte-poor PRP are in knee osteoarthritis. A Japanese randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial tested leukocyte-poor PRP in mild to moderate knee osteoarthritis [5]. A 2024 double-blind randomized trial found leukocytes did not influence safety or efficacy in knee osteoarthritis [3]. The 2021 RESTORE randomized trial compared PRP with placebo for knee pain and cartilage [6]. No trial found here compared leukocyte-poor and leukocyte-rich PRP for hair or facial appearance.

timeline.event: A classification separates pure PRP (P-PRP) from leukocyte-rich platelet concentrates [2].
